messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 21-year-old African American woman who came to treatment in the first year after returning from combat deployment. Before enlistment, and even during training, she had thought of herself as steady under pressure, the person other people trusted with difficult conversations; that identity had carried naturally into her current work as a counselor. The event she returns to most often happened during a night operation. The area had dropped into near-total darkness except for intermittent aircraft light and the heavy chopping sound of helicopters overhead. In the confusion, there had been a brief exchange about getting word to someone’s family if the team did not make it back, and that detail fixed itself in her mind alongside the darkness and the aircraft noise. Since then, those elements have not felt like neutral reminders. They land as if they are pulling her straight back toward the moment when she believes something in her failed.

In the weeks after returning home, Amina found that comments about family could unsettle her abruptly. Even routine conversations at work, when a client mentioned a mother calling too often or a coworker joked about family drama, could make her chest tighten and her attention narrow. If she left the office after sunset and had to cross a dim parking lot, or if a helicopter passed overhead, she felt the same jolt. In those moments she did not only feel frightened; she also became harshly certain about what the reminders meant. She had come to believe there was something about her that made the event happen, that someone more competent would not have ended up in that situation, and that the version of herself she respected—the capable, reliable one—was gone. The trigger was not just a cue; it seemed to prove, again and again, her own defectiveness.

She started organizing her life around preventing that collapse. Because family talk had become so charged, she withdrew from people she had socialized with before deployment, especially those likely to ask about home or to compare who she was now with who she had been. At work as a counselor, she became skilled at redirecting conversations away from anything that sounded too close to family loss or reunion, and she volunteered for tasks that let her stay behind a closed office door rather than chat in shared spaces. She stopped trying to build new friendships and shut down early signs of romantic interest, convinced she no longer had the capacity to be the person others would expect. She also stopped watching films and television that involved war, military scenes, or even rescue aircraft, because the risk of hearing rotor blades in a living room felt intolerable.

These efforts brought short-term relief, but over months they narrowed her world and deepened the meaning she made of what had happened. The less she saw old friends, the less chance she had to experience herself as more than the person from that night. Avoiding new relationships left her increasingly alone with the thought that no one who really knew her now would see her as capable. Steering away from media that touched anything similar kept the whole subject feeling dangerous and unfinished. She took the fact that she needed so many precautions as evidence that she truly was no longer able to do the things that once defined her. Each retreat seemed to confirm her private comparison: somebody else would have handled this better, recovered faster, and gone back to living.

Her avoidance also made the triggers spread and sharpen. Because she kept refusing dim restaurants, evening gatherings, and post-work invitations, ordinary darkness remained unfamiliar and menacing. Because she changed the channel or left the room whenever aircraft sounds came on, even a distant helicopter over the city could stop her cold. Because she cut herself off from social contacts, comments about family at work struck with even greater force; she had no buffer, no ordinary conversation in which “family” could mean anything other than the charged fragment she carries from deployment. In session she described feeling ambushed by small things that other people do not even notice, then hating herself for being ambushed at all.

By the time she sought help, the strain was showing in her job and daily life. She was still functioning enough to keep working as a counselor, but she had begun arranging her schedule to avoid late hours, declining collegial lunches, and leaving break rooms when conversation turned personal. She is single, and what troubles her is not only that she feels lonely but that she has started to see loneliness as safer and more fitting for who she is now. She came to treatment after realizing she was building her entire life around not hearing, not seeing, not being asked. What frightens her most is the possibility that this withdrawn, diminished version of herself is permanent; what she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is that she might learn how to be in the world again without every dark space, helicopter, or family remark turning into proof that she is to blame and no longer capable.
